href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#description-does-not-necessarily-seek-associations
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
section: Description Does Not Necessarily Seek Associations
text:
Description Does Not Necessarily Seek Associations


Description examines distributions of single variables: middle, spread, shape, count, and proportion.
It supports resource management and planning.
Examples:

How many ventilators are available in Texas?
What is the average age of people living in Florida?
How much time elapses, on average, between exposure to a pathogen and the occurrence of disease symptoms?

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#description-can-also-compare-distributions
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#description-can-also-compare-distributions
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Description Can Also Compare Distributions


Sometimes description does look for associations.
It may compare distributions of single variables within levels of another variable.
Examples:

Are more ventilators available in Texas or New York?
Are people older, on average, in Florida or Pennsylvania?
Is symptom onset quicker, on average, for cholera or E. coli?

text:
Closed and Open Populations



CLOSED POPULATION

After the population is defined, it does not add new members over time.
It loses members only to death.



OPEN POPULATION

It may gain members through birth or as people meet the membership definition.
It loses members as people stop meeting the criteria or die.




Source: (Lash et al. 2021)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#source-and-target-populations
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#source-and-target-populations
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Source and Target Populations

Source population: The population from which persons will be sampled and included in a measurement of disease frequency.

The source population of the original Framingham Heart Study included men and women aged 30 to 62 who were residents of Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1948.

Target population: The group of people about which the scientific or public-health question asks and for whom the disease-frequency information will be relevant, we hope.

Information about cardiac-disease risk factors from the Framingham Heart Study contributed to a nearly 75% decline in cardiovascular-disease mortality in most industrialized societies.


Sources: (Lash et al. 2021; Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#study-population-and-sample
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#study-population-and-sample
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Study Population and Sample

Study population: The subset, up to a complete census, of the source population whose experience is included in a measurement of disease frequency.

In the Framingham Heart Study, not everyone eligible was invited and not everyone invited agreed. Those who were invited, agreed, and were free of prevalent cardiovascular disease constituted the study population.

Sample: A selected subset of a population. A sample may be random or nonrandom and representative or nonrepresentative.

Sources: (Lash et al. 2021; Porta 2008)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#cohorts
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#cohorts
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Cohorts


A cohort is a group of persons whose membership is defined permanently, or a population in which satisfying a set of defining events makes membership permanent.
The term is often used as a synonym for “sample” in a cohort study.
Every cohort member is enumerated: known or listed. This is not necessarily true of a closed population.


Source: (Lash et al. 2021)

text:
Terminology Recap: Population Types









Term
Definition
Example




Population
A group of people during a defined time period who share characteristics or meet membership criteria.
The population of the United States.


Closed population
After the population is defined, it adds no new members and loses members only to death.
People who had a flu vaccine in 2022.


Open population
During a defined time frame, it gains members through birth or newly met criteria and/or loses members when criteria are no longer met or through loss to follow-up.
People who have the flu.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-describes-existing-conditions
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-describes-existing-conditions
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Describes Existing Conditions


Prevalence provides information about the presence or absence of a condition of interest, such as a disease, exposure, or characteristic, in a population.
It describes the extent to which the condition is present in a population during a given time frame.
Asking about the prevalence of diabetes means asking how many, or more likely what proportion, of people currently living in the population have diabetes.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-count
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-count
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Count


A count of people in a population with the condition of interest during a given time frame.
As few as 0 people and as many as all people can be living with the condition.
Range: 0 to infinity.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Proportion


The proportion or percentage of the population that presently has the condition of interest or presently has a history of the condition during a specified period, such as a history of cancer in the past 10 years.
Since none, some, or all population members can have the condition or a history of it, prevalence proportion ranges from 0 to 1, much like a probability.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion-formula
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion-formula
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Proportion: Formula

\[
\text{Prevalence proportion} = \frac{\text{Count with the condition}}{\text{Living members of the population}}
\]

href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#point-prevalence-and-period-prevalence
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Point Prevalence and Period Prevalence


Point prevalence: prevalence of a condition of interest at a single point in time.
Period prevalence: prevalence of a condition of interest over a period of time.
As the duration of the period shrinks, period prevalence converges to point prevalence.
There is no hard-and-fast rule for what window is sufficiently short to count as point prevalence.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-odds
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-odds
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Odds


Prevalence odds is a simple function of prevalence proportion, just as odds in general is a simple function of probability.
It is typically reported for convenience or desirable statistical properties.
Prevalence odds is prevalence proportion divided by 1 minus prevalence proportion.
Range: 0 to infinity.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-odds-formula
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-odds-formula
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Odds: Formula

\[
\text{Prevalence odds} = \frac{\text{Prevalence proportion}}{1 - \text{Prevalence proportion}}
\]

Among the members of the population, the odds of disease in month 2 were 0.25.

href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-describes-new-occurrences
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Describes New Occurrences


Prevalence measures how many cases are present at a moment or over a period; incidence measures how many new cases arise over a specified period.
Unlike prevalence, incidence measures occurrences or events: transitions from a condition being absent in an individual to the condition being present over a specified period.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion-and-risk
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion-and-risk
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Proportion and Risk


Incidence proportion and “risk” are sometimes used interchangeably in epidemiology.
Risk can be ambiguous. Incidence proportion is less so.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-count
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-count
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Count


A count of new occurrences of a condition in a population at risk for the occurrence during a given time frame.
Range: 0 to infinity.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Proportion


The proportion of the population that experiences a new occurrence of the condition among those at risk of experiencing a new occurrence during a given time frame.
Like all proportions, it falls between 0 and 1.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion-formula
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion-formula
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Proportion: Formula

\[
\text{Incidence proportion} = \frac{\text{Count of new occurrences}}{\text{Population at risk}}
\]

href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion-over-12-months
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Proportion Over 12 Months




5 people developed disease.
9 people were at risk at baseline.
Person 1 was already diseased and therefore not at risk for a new occurrence.



\[
\frac{5}{9} = 0.56 = 56\%
\]

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#interpreting-incidence-proportion
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#interpreting-incidence-proportion
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Interpreting Incidence Proportion

Among the members of the population, the incidence of disease over 12 months of follow-up was 0.56.
Fifty-six percent of the population developed disease over 12 months of follow-up.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-odds-formula
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-odds-formula
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Odds: Formula

\[
\text{Incidence odds} = \frac{\text{Incidence proportion}}{1 - \text{Incidence proportion}}
\]

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Odds Over 12 Months

\[
\text{Incidence odds} = \frac{0.56}{1 - 0.56} = 1.27
\]

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#interpreting-incidence-odds
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#interpreting-incidence-odds
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Interpreting Incidence Odds

Among the members of the population, the odds of incident disease over 12 months of follow-up were 1.27.
For every 127 people who developed incident disease over 12 months of follow-up, 100 people did not.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-rate
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-rate
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Rate


A measure of the average intensity at which an event occurs in people’s experience over time.
For a population followed from baseline, it is the number of cases divided by the person-time at risk accumulated by the population.
Range: 0 to infinity.
Not a proportion.
The denominator is reciprocal time, usually person-time.
The numeric value depends on the selected time unit and therefore has no interpretation by itself.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#person-time
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#person-time
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Person-Time

Person-time is the amount of time observed for all people under study while they are at risk of experiencing an incident outcome.

Source: (Westreich 2019)

text:
Incidence Rate: Calculation

\[
\text{Incidence rate} = \frac{\text{Count of new occurrences}}{\text{Person-time at risk}}
\]
\[
= \frac{5}{64\text{ person-months}} \approx 7.8\text{ per 100 person-months}
\]

Interpreting the Incidence Rate

The incidence rate of disease among the members of the population was 5 cases per 64 person-months during 12 months of follow-up.
Equivalently, the incidence rate was 7.8 cases per 100 person-months during 12 months of follow-up.

href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#course-learning-objectives
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Course Learning objectives

Define epidemiology and key associated terminology, especially confounding.
Distinguish among association, prediction, and causation.
Explain the Rothman model of sufficient-component causes (RMSCC) and the concept of multifactorial causation.
Explain the limitations of anecdotal evidence in drawing epidemiologic conclusions.
Explain why disseminating risk information is sometimes necessary but rarely sufficient to improve population health.


By the end of this course, my goal is for you to be able to:

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#lecture-learning-objectives
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#lecture-learning-objectives
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Lecture Learning objectives
By the end of this lesson, you’ll be able to:

Define epidemiology and explain its core assumptions.
Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology.
Differentiate epidemic, endemic, and pandemic patterns of disease occurrence.
Describe at least three applications of epidemiology in public health practice.

Opening Question


What is Epidemiology?


Respond here



The study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events (e.g. infectious disease) in specified (human) populations and the application of this study to control health problems Reveal the answer: after_discussion. Show the distribution: yes. Responses are anonymous. If polling fails: Read the question aloud, then take a show of hands for each option in turn and record the counts on the whiteboard.

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#what-is-epidemiology
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#what-is-epidemiology
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
What is Epidemiology?

EPIDEMIOLOGY

epi – “on, upon”
demo – “people”
ology – “study of”

Definition: Epidemiology is concerned with the distribution and determinants of health and diseases, morbidity, injuries, disability, and mortality in populations. Epidemiologic studies are applied to the control of health problems in populations (Quinlan 2025).

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#scenario-exercise
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#scenario-exercise
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Scenario Exercise



Scenario: A city health department notices that one neighborhood has twice the rate of asthma ER visits in another neighborhood in the same city. This difference has been observed every year for the past three years.
Questions: Do you think this difference is mostly due to random chance—yes or no? If it’s not random, what might explain the difference?
What are we assuming if we believe those factors matter?

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#assumptions-of-epidemiology
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#assumptions-of-epidemiology
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Assumptions of Epidemiology


ASSUMPTION 1
Human disease does not occur at random
Disease frequency and distribution vary because of identifiable factors that increase or decrease risk.


ASSUMPTION 2
Determinants of disease can be identified
Causal and preventive factors can be studied through systematic investigation of populations.



Talk about distribution and determinants, and why that’s harder than it sounds at first. Use my own research in EM and Parkinson’s as examples.

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#descriptive-and-analytic-epidemiology
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#descriptive-and-analytic-epidemiology
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Descriptive and Analytic Epidemiology


DISTRIBUTION
Descriptive epidemiology

When was the population affected?
Where was the population affected?
Who was affected?



DETERMINANTS
Analytic epidemiology

How was the population affected?
Why was the population affected?




Talk about confounding

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#micro-activity-thinking-like-an-epidemiologist
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#micro-activity-thinking-like-an-epidemiologist
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Micro-Activity: Thinking Like an Epidemiologist

Watch the short video on John Snow and cholera. John Snow: Pioneer of Epidemiology
As you watch, focus on these questions:
What patterns did Snow observe? (Who, where, when — descriptive epidemiology)
What explanation was he testing? (How, why — analytic epidemiology)
Descriptive epidemiology often comes first; analytic epidemiology builds on it.


[Sources] - PBS LearningMedia, John Snow: Pioneer of Epidemiology, https://kera.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/envh10.sci.life.nathis.johnsnow/john-snow-pioneer-of-epidemiology/ (inherited link). [/Sources]

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#history-of-epidemiology-key-events
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#history-of-epidemiology-key-events
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
History of Epidemiology: Key Events









Event
Time Period
Description




Bubonic Plague Epidemics (Black Death)
1347 - 1351
One of the deadliest pandemics, causing 75–200 million deaths in Eurasia.


Development of Toxicology
16th Century
Paracelsus, “Father of Toxicology,” introduced the principle: “The dose makes the poison.”


Development of Biostatistics
18th Century
John Graunt pioneered statistical analysis, using Bills of Mortality to study disease patterns in London.


Development of Smallpox Vaccine
1796
Edward Jenner created the first vaccine by using cowpox to confer immunity to smallpox.


1918 Influenza Pandemic
1918-19
The “Spanish flu” infected a third of the global population, killing 50–100 million.


Identification of Smoking as a Cause of Cancer
1950
Landmark studies linked smoking to lung cancer, driving public health campaigns against tobacco use.


Eradication of Smallpox
1980
WHO declared smallpox eradicated, marking the success of global vaccination efforts.





You do not need to memorize these, but let’s talk about why they are important.
Talk about the demographic transition and epidemiologic transition when you discuss the history of epidemiology.

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#disease-distribution-patterns
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#disease-distribution-patterns
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Disease Distribution Patterns


01
Endemic
Disease or condition consistently present in a population

Relatively stable over time
Expected level of occurrence in a given place



02
Epidemic (Outbreak)
Disease occurrence in excess of what is normally expected

Sudden increase over a short period
Often limited to a specific region



03
Pandemic
An epidemic that spreads across multiple countries or continents

Global distribution
Affects a large proportion of the population

href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#quiz-epidemic-01
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Exercise: Disease Distribution Patterns


Ebola virus cases in parts of Africa exceed what is normally expected for that region. In this situation, the Ebola virus was [a/an] ________.


A. endemic
B. epidemic
C. pandemic


Respond here



Answer: B. An epidemic is the occurrence of disease cases above what is normally expected in a population or region. Reveal the answer: after_discussion. Show the distribution: yes. Responses are anonymous. If polling fails: Read the question aloud, then take a show of hands for each option in turn and record the counts on the whiteboard.

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#quiz-endemic-01
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#quiz-endemic-01
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Exercise: Disease Distribution Patterns


Malaria is always present in Africa due to the presence of infected mosquitoes. In this situation, malaria is [a/an] ________.


A. endemic
B. epidemic
C. pandemic


Respond here



Answer: A. An endemic disease is consistently present at an expected baseline level in a population or region. Reveal the answer: after_discussion. Show the distribution: yes. Responses are anonymous. If polling fails: Read the question aloud, then take a show of hands for each option in turn and record the counts on the whiteboard.

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#quiz-pandemic-01
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#quiz-pandemic-01
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Exercise: Disease Distribution Patterns


Between 2019 and 2023, the SARS-CoV-2 virus infected more than 600 million people worldwide. In this situation, the SARS-CoV-2 virus was [a/an] ________.


A. endemic
B. epidemic
C. pandemic


Respond here



Answer: C. A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across countries or continents and affects a large number of people. Reveal the answer: after_discussion. Show the distribution: yes. Responses are anonymous. If polling fails: Read the question aloud, then take a show of hands for each option in turn and record the counts on the whiteboard.

text:
Use of Epidemiology
In the first group presentation for this course, you will:
Describe a health problem
(Who is affected? Where? When?)
Explain possible reasons
(Risk factors or exposures)
Interpret evidence
(Patterns and associations)
Propose prevention or control strategies

Students may leave or work on group projects.
